scores.claim_text: Two CoreWeave data center leases (250 MW total) + 150 MW option at Polaris Forge 1, Ellendale ND, executed May 28 / July 24, 2025.
supports: FY25 10-K Item 1 Business and Subsequent Events disclose the leases with CoreWeave by name; the 10-K is signed/audited
FY26 Q3 10-Q (filed Apr 8 2026) confirms HPC Hosting Business commenced operations at Polaris Forge 1 Building 1 and recognized $182.3M HPC revenue YTD
scores.M_check: edgar_fts.query_fulltext(search_term='Ellendale'/'Polaris Forge'/'CoreWeave'); restricted to MSFT, AMZN, META, GOOGL, AAPL, ORCL, NVDA, AMD CIKs
scores.M_value: Ellendale: 197 hits all-filers, 0 external (all APLD-self); Polaris Forge: 44 hits all-filers, 0 external; CoreWeave: 0 hits at AMZN/MSFT/META/GOOGL/AAPL/ORCL/AMD, 7 hits at NVDA (Nvidia equity stake context). Hyperscaler counterparty CIKs return 0 for Ellendale/Polaris Forge/Applied Digital.
scores.interpretation: Per Calibration Heuristic 7 (counterparty disclosure threshold) CoreWeave-named contracts are UNVERIFIABLE on the counterparty axis because CoreWeave was still a private company at cutoff and would not appear in EDGAR as a registrant. The lease was filed by APLD itself; the counterparty cannot independently corroborate via EDGAR. Operational evidence (Q3 FY26 10-Q showing $44.1M base rent recognized in three months) supports that Building 1 is energized and generating revenue, which is consistent with the lease being real. No basis to call this a red flag, but no independent counterparty validation possible either.

scores.claim_text: 286 MW crypto-hosting capacity operating at full capacity, single anchor customer, $144.2M FY25 segment revenue.
supports: 10-K Properties section names APLD ELN-01 LLC owning land in Ellendale; subsidiary structure is concrete
10-K segment table shows $142.3M base + $1.9M related-party = $144.2M Data Center Hosting Business revenue FY25 (versus $136.6M FY24, $55.4M FY23) — consistent with a 286 MW operating base scaling
FY26 Q3 10-Q confirms continued operation with $12.8M YTD revenue increase in Data Center Hosting
scores.M_check: edgar_fts.query_fulltext for 'Jamestown' (1146 generic hits, common toponym; not discriminating) and '286 MW' (35 generic hits)
scores.M_value: Operating-MW claims are consistent with FY25 segment revenue arithmetic ($144M / 286 MW / 12 months = ~$42K/MW-month, in line with crypto-hosting price points). No counterparty needed because the claim is a self-operating-capacity claim and the financial statements corroborate it.
scores.interpretation: Operating-MW with bookings that show up as recognized revenue is a stage-6 (revenue-generating) claim per the AI-DC stage ladder. The crypto-mining anchor exists (one customer accounts for revenue concentration). No red flag, but the 2.5-year remaining contract term means there is meaningful re-pricing/re-tenanting risk before mid-2028; that is disclosed and not a contradiction.

scores.claim_text: January 13, 2025 Unit Purchase Agreement with Macquarie Asset Management (MIP VI HPC Holdings, LLC) to sell HPC Hosting Business interest, conditioned on hyperscaler lease execution at the first 100 MW of Polaris Forge 1.
supports: 10-K explicitly discloses the UPA, conditions, and a series of extensions (April 4, 2025 deadline extension; October 13, 2025 termination backstop)
MAM consent dated May 21, 2025 permitted the CoreWeave leases — but the UPA closing condition required a 'hyperscaler' counterparty (in a form acceptable to MAM)

FY26 Q3 10-Q (Apr 8, 2026) makes NO mention of the MIP VI HPC Holdings UPA and reclassifies HPC Hosting as a 'core' segment in continuing operations (rather than as 'held for sale'), suggesting the UPA terminated unsigned by the Oct 13, 2025 backstop
scores.M_check: edgar_fts.query_fulltext for 'MIP VI HPC' (16 hits, all APLD self-filings) and 'APLD HPC Holdings' (29 hits, all APLD self-filings); no third-party Macquarie disclosure of closing
scores.M_value: Zero external Macquarie or MAM filer corroboration of UPA closing. The 10-Q omits the UPA entirely. The Macquarie Equipment Capital promissory note (Dec 18, 2025) is a separate debt facility (parent guarantee, equipment financing) — not the equity sale-of-HPC-Hosting UPA.
scores.interpretation: The 'sale of HPC Hosting to Macquarie' did NOT close (CoreWeave is not the hyperscaler form MAM contemplated; the deadline lapsed). APLD continues to consolidate HPC Hosting and is borrowing rather than selling. This is a MODERATE under-delivery against the FY25-headline plan; not strictly a contradiction because the filing disclosed the conditions, but the realized outcome (no equity-sale closing) is a strategic reversal that meaningfully changes the company's path to monetizing the build. Capital intensity (the $1.1B YTD CapEx increase) is now being funded by APLD instead of being shared with MAM.

scores.claim_text: HPC Hosting Business has a single counterparty (CoreWeave) on 15-year leases for 100% of contracted base, with no diversification.
supports: 10-K: 'We currently have one customer in this business segment, which is a party to two fifteen-year term leases with us.'

10-Q March 30, 2026 amendments: CoreWeave assigned the Building 3 lease to CoreWeave SPV (Compute Acquisition Co. VIII), substituted SPV for parent on Building 3 in full, suspended two of four data halls of Building 2; CoreWeave parent is now a springing (not direct) guarantor on the SPV's obligations, with only a $50M LC to back Building 2
Macquarie UPA's hyperscaler-form lease condition was not met by the CoreWeave lease itself
scores.M_check: edgar_fts.query_fulltext for CoreWeave at hyperscaler CIKs (only NVDA shows mentions, which relate to Nvidia's equity stake in CoreWeave, not customer relationship). Per heuristic 7 CoreWeave is private; no EDGAR corroboration possible on counterparty axis.
scores.M_value: UNVERIFIABLE on counterparty corroboration axis. Self-disclosed structure is internally consistent.
scores.interpretation: MODERATE because (a) the entire HPC story is single-counterparty risk on a still-private neocloud (CoreWeave's own financial health is itself dependent on hyperscaler demand and Nvidia capacity allocation); (b) the March 30, 2026 SPV substitution + springing guaranty is a clear credit-quality DETERIORATION versus the original FY25 disclosure (originally APLD subsidiaries each had a direct CoreWeave parent lease; now Building 3 is wholly with the SPV and the parent only springs in conditionally). This is the textbook AI-DC counterparty-quality erosion the calibration framework asks us to track. Not yet RED_FLAG_NEGATIVE because operational revenue is in fact being recognized and CoreWeave has not defaulted, but the trend is unfavorable and the lease economics depend on a counterparty whose credit cannot be independently verified.

scores.claim_text: Material weakness in ICFR (complex financial instruments) and DCP not effective as of May 31, 2025; multiple prior material weaknesses (segregation of duties, related party transactions, financial reporting process) have been remediated.
supports: 10-K Item 9A admits 'our disclosure controls and procedures were not effective as of May 31, 2025'
Three prior material weaknesses are reported as remediated, but a new one was identified for the most-recent fiscal year

The same weakness (complex financial instruments) is the proximate cause of the $89.6M loss on the conversion-option derivative due to authorized-shares shortfall — a self-confirmed control failure with quantified dollar impact
scores.M_check: Internal claim; M-source corroboration not informative (ICFR opinions are self-reported by the company and auditor). No external query meaningfully tests this.
scores.M_value: N/A (self-disclosed). Internal-consistency check shows the $89.6M conversion-option derivative loss is a tangible consequence.
scores.interpretation: MODERATE: this is a non-trivial open control gap on a company with $450M of convertibles and several preferred series in flight. The same control area (complex financial instruments) directly produced an $89.6M loss event in FY25, so the weakness is not merely theoretical. Management commits to remediation in H1 FY26 but as of the cutoff the remediation has not been validated. Trend (three prior weaknesses remediated, one new one) is mixed. Per heuristic 10 distress fingerprints, repeated material-weakness churn alongside heavy dilutive issuance is consistent with a structurally stretched balance sheet.

scores.claim_text: Capital structure: $450M 2.75% Convertibles (June 2030), $375M SMBC Loan (August 2026 maturity), Macquarie/SMBC refinancing chain, $160M PIPE at $3.24, multiple preferred series (E/E-1/F/G), $193.9M post-balance-sheet ATM, $231M FY25 net loss; share count went from 114M weighted-avg FY24 to 201M FY25.
supports: 10-K Note 7 debt schedule with $869M total debt and $386M FY27 maturity wall (driven by $375M SMBC Loan that matures August 2026)

Weighted-avg diluted shares 114M -> 201M FY24->FY25 (76% dilution in one fiscal year), with another 46M shares of potential convertible-note dilution, 21.7M preferred-conversion shares, and 14.1M unvested RSU dilution overhanging at year-end
Six separate capital raises in the 12 months covered by the 10-K (PIPE, Series E, E-1, F, G, Convertibles, YA Fund, CIM Promissory Note, Macquarie Promissory Note, SMBC Loan)
Repeated short-tenor bridge facilities (CIM -> Macquarie -> SMBC) within one fiscal year
$89.6M derivative loss from running out of authorized shares mid-conversion
scores.M_check: Internal-disclosure claim; no useful EDGAR third-party query.
scores.M_value: N/A. The stack of issuances is self-evident from the 10-K.
scores.interpretation: SEVERE per heuristic 10 distress fingerprints. The pattern -- repeated bridge financings within 12 months, 76% one-year share-count dilution, running out of authorized shares mid-derivative-settlement, August 2026 SMBC wall against a still-not-yet-cash-flow-positive HPC build, and reliance on continued ATM sales -- is consistent with a structurally undercapitalized issuer that needs the HPC ramp to proceed without delays in order to refinance. The FY26 Q3 10-Q shows $1.1B YTD investing-CapEx, which intensifies (not relieves) the financing pressure. The framework should treat this as a high-base-rate distress profile, especially given that the Macquarie equity sale fell through.

scores.claim_text: March 30, 2026 CoreWeave lease restructuring: Building 2 term suspended on two of four data halls (replaced by a parallel SPV lease); Building 3 lease assigned entirely to CoreWeave SPV (Compute Acquisition Co. VIII) with only a springing parent guaranty plus a $50M letter of credit.
supports: FY26 Q3 10-Q Subsequent Events: 'suspend the term for two of the four data halls covered by the lease' on Building 2; full assignment of Building 3 to CoreWeave SPV; springing (not direct) parent guaranty; $50M letter of credit

Compared to the FY25 10-K disclosure (APLD guaranteed APLD ELN-02 and ELN-03 obligations to CoreWeave parent on both leases), the FY26 amendment SHIFTS counterparty risk: CoreWeave parent's direct exposure is reduced; APLD's exposure to a thinly-capitalized SPV is increased
scores.M_check: edgar_fts.query_fulltext for 'springing guaranty' (73 hits across REITs - structurally a real-estate financing concept, not unprecedented; confirms the term is used in arms-length real estate transactions but does not validate the economic substance for APLD-CoreWeave specifically)
scores.M_value: Counterparty corroboration unavailable (CoreWeave private). The springing-guaranty structure is real-estate-standard but represents a credit-quality concession by APLD relative to the original parent-guaranteed leases.
scores.interpretation: SEVERE per heuristic 7 logic adapted for an UNVERIFIABLE counterparty. The economic substance is: 14 months after signing, CoreWeave (a) suspended half the term on half the data halls of Building 2, (b) substituted an SPV with a springing-only parent guaranty on Building 3. This is a clear weakening of CoreWeave's commitment to take MW. The framework's stage-ladder (term sheet -> definitive lease -> shell -> commissioning -> energized -> revenue-generating) shows Building 1 is at stage 6 but Building 2 partially regressed from stage 2 (definitive lease) toward stage 1.5 (SPV-substituted lease with springing guaranty). The fact that the FY25 10-K headlined '400 MW signed with CoreWeave' just nine months before this restructuring is a disclosure-quality issue: the headline TCV / MW number was already softening at the time of filing but was not flagged as such. SEVERE under heuristic 9 (TCV vs current-period revenue conflation) because the 400 MW figure was used in the headline without disclosing the assignability/substitution rights that ultimately got exercised.

scores.claim_text: FY26 YTD HPC revenue of $182.3M (Building 1 operating), of which $118.2M (65%) is tenant fit-out services, $55.7M (30%) is base rent, $8.4M (5%) is power pass-through. Q3 split is 28% fit-out / 62% rent / 11% pass-through.
supports: FY26 Q3 10-Q MD&A explicitly breaks out the components

Cost of revenues line shows $112.5M YTD increase 'in expenses associated with tenant fit-out services' -- meaning approximately $112.5M of $118.2M (95%) of fit-out revenue is pass-through cost. Fit-out is a low-margin construction-installation activity dressed up as 'revenue' in segment commentary.
scores.M_check: Internal MD&A consistency check; no external M-source applicable.
scores.M_value: Margin arithmetic: $182.3M rev - $112.5M fit-out cost ~ $69.8M segment-equivalent gross profit, while the segment reports $12.9M operating profit. Fit-out is essentially a wash. The recurring base-rent + power-pass-through line ($64.1M YTD) is the more economically meaningful number.
scores.interpretation: MODERATE per heuristic 9 (TCV vs current-period revenue conflation) AND heuristic 11 (revenue-recognition pattern). Reporting tenant fit-out at gross (as $118M of revenue with offsetting cost of revenues) inflates the apparent top-line ramp of the HPC business in headline numbers; the true recurring run-rate is $44.1M base-rent + $8.1M pass-through in Q3 (annualized $208M), not the headline 'HPC revenue of $71M/quarter -> $284M/year'. Not severe because the company does break out the components in MD&A, but a careful reader is required to find them; press releases and many analyst summaries cite the headline number.
